questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Describe the different types of rocks that result from the progressive regional metamorphism of shale.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Regional metamorphism** affects very large areas along **convergent plate boundaries (mountain building)**, where **both temperature and directed pressure** increase. When **shale (or mudstone)** is subjected to **progressively higher grades**, it is changed in turn into the following rocks (the **prograde sequence**), each with characteristic **minerals and texture**.

1. **Slate (low grade, about 200 to 300 degrees Celsius).** A very fine-grained, hard, dark grey rock. Clay minerals recrystallise to tiny **chlorite and sericite (white mica)**. The flat mineral grains are aligned at right angles to the pressure, giving **slaty cleavage**, so the rock splits into thin, flat sheets (roofing slates) which may cut across the original bedding. Grains are too small to see.
2. **Phyllite (low to medium grade, about 300 to 400 degrees Celsius).** The mica grows a little larger and gives a **silky sheen or lustre** on the cleavage surfaces; the rock is still fine-grained, with a wavy or crinkled foliation (**phyllitic texture**).
3. **Schist (medium grade, about 400 to 600 degrees Celsius).** **Coarse-grained, with visible flaky minerals** (muscovite, **biotite**) strongly aligned, giving **schistosity**, a rock that splits along wavy planes. **Porphyroblasts** of index minerals appear, with increasing grade: **garnet, staurolite, kyanite** (the garnet or kyanite schist).
4. **Gneiss (high grade, above about 600 degrees Celsius).** Coarse, **banded** rock with alternate light bands (**quartz and feldspar**) and dark bands (**biotite, hornblende, sillimanite**): **gneissic banding** or foliation formed by segregation of the minerals. Little aligned mica remains, so it does not split easily.
5. **Migmatite (very high grade, at the beginning of melting).** A mixed rock in which streaks and veins of light, coarse granite-like material (formed by **partial melting**) are mixed with dark gneissic or schistose material. At higher temperatures complete melting gives granitic magma.

**Index minerals and zones (Barrow's zones):** chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite appear in this order as the grade rises. In summary, as the **grade increases**, the **grain size increases**, the **mineral assemblage changes** to higher-temperature minerals (water-bearing minerals are replaced by dry ones), and the texture changes from **slaty cleavage to schistosity and then banding**.

*Sketch to draw:* a simple column or a block showing shale, slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss in order of increasing grade, with the mineral names, the direction of pressure and the foliation planes.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Outline a classification of faults based on dip values and the apparent relative movement of the faulted blocks.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **fault** is a fracture in rock along which the two sides (blocks) have **moved relative to one another**. The inclined fault plane has a **hanging wall** (the block above the plane) and a **footwall** (the block below). Faults are classified by the **dip of the fault plane** and by the **apparent relative movement** of the blocks.

**1. Normal faults (dip-slip, tensional).** The **hanging wall has moved down** relative to the footwall. The dip is **steep, usually more than 45 degrees** (commonly 50 to 70 degrees), and the faulting **lengthens the crust** (tension, divergent boundaries). Associated features: **graben (rift valley, a block dropped between two normal faults)** and **horst (a raised block)**, and fault scarps.

**2. Reverse faults (dip-slip, compressional).** The **hanging wall has moved up** relative to the footwall. The dip is **high, more than 45 degrees**, and the faulting **shortens the crust** (compression, convergent boundaries).

**3. Thrust faults (low-angle reverse faults).** The **hanging wall has moved up** as for a reverse fault, but the dip is **low, less than about 45 degrees** (in an overthrust or nappe, less than about 10 degrees), so that older rocks are pushed a long distance over younger rocks. They are typical of **intense compression in fold mountains**, and can produce klippen and windows (inliers).

**4. Strike-slip faults (wrench or tear faults).** The movement is **horizontal, along the strike** of the near-vertical fault plane (dip about 80 to 90 degrees), with no important vertical movement. Facing the fault, if the opposite block appears to have moved to the **right it is dextral (right-lateral)**; to the **left, sinistral (left-lateral)**. A **transform fault** is a large strike-slip fault at a plate boundary (San Andreas fault).

**5. Oblique-slip faults.** The movement has **both a dip-slip and a strike-slip component** (the slip direction lies between the dip and the strike). **Hinge (rotational) faults** are those in which the displacement increases along the fault from a pivot point.

**In summary:**

| Type | Dip of fault plane | Apparent movement | Stress |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | steep (above about 45 degrees) | hanging wall down | tension |
| Reverse | steep (above about 45 degrees) | hanging wall up | compression |
| Thrust | gentle (below about 45 degrees) | hanging wall up over the footwall | strong compression |
| Strike-slip | vertical or near vertical | horizontal, dextral or sinistral | shear |
| Oblique-slip | any | combined dip and strike movement | combined |

*Sketches to draw:* block diagrams of a normal fault, a reverse fault, a thrust and a strike-slip fault with the hanging wall, footwall, dip angle and arrows of relative movement labelled.
